a.title:
VR Cinematics
for UE 5.8
a.subtitle: Record it in VR. Re-shoot it from anywhere. Render it once.
a.thesis: A VR recording is a set, not a finished film. Measure its problems, fix them with three ideas, and put new cameras in it.
a.takeaway: A recording is a set. Put a new camera in it.
a.cover_spoken: Welcome. Recording is on; links are in chat. Questions in chat, answered at the two breaks.

b.title:
How We Built the Cameras
for A Christmas Carol VR
b.subtitle: From a spacebar to a cinematographer build
b.thesis: Treat the camera as data: a shot is a struct, a show is a recording, and a cut is a credited decision.
b.takeaway: Cameras are data. Shots are structs. Credit the operator.
b.cover_spoken: Conference cut of Part VI of the class: the Christmas Carol camera case study.

pool.title: By 1 pm you will have made this
pool.alt: A twenty-second edit cut from five virtual cameras re-shooting one recorded VR take: a stabilized first-person view, over-the-shoulder, orbit, locked-off and low hero shots.
pool.credit: Class practice take, re-shot and rendered with the VR Cinematics kit · Alex Coulombe Presents
pool.notes: Play this cold, with no intro. Twenty seconds. Then say: this is one recorded take of someone moving around in VR, and every shot you just saw is a new camera we added afterward. By one o'clock you will have done this from your own take. The four things to leave with: measure the shake, cut on teleports, level the horizon, and start a draft render before we hit the final. ALEX TO CONFIRM: the instructor on the day (the kit's run-of-show is written so a substitute can teach it).

pool.title:
Raw VR
Footage
Looks Bad.
pool.tagline: Four problems, and one take we can measure.
pool.notes: Part one is why you can't just publish what a headset records. Run of show 0:10 to 0:20.

Four problems. Shake: tracking noise and hand tremor at 72 to 120 Hz. Tilt: head roll tips the horizon, and roll is the biggest nausea source. Jump: teleports and snap turns are instant cuts the viewer never chose. FOV: the headset sees about 100 degrees and a 16:9 screen does not, so the framing was never meant for a flat frame. Hold the four words on screen and ask the chat which one they notice most in their own captures.

pool.title: Same Take, Two Cameras
pool.subtitle: Drag the line
pool.altA: A recorded VR head camera: the horizon tilts and the view trembles
pool.altB: The same moment after stabilization: the horizon is level and the view is steady
pool.credit: Class practice take · VR Cinematics kit · Alex Coulombe Presents
pool.notes: Drag the line across. Left is the recorded head camera, right is the same moment after the class tool. Same take, same frame. Don't explain the method yet: just let them see that the right side is a camera you could put in a trailer. Then play the next slide, which is the same comparison in motion.

pool.alt: Side by side: the recorded head camera on the left, jittery with a tilted horizon, and the stabilized camera on the right, steady and level. The same twenty-second take.
pool.credit: Class practice take · jitter 1.54 to 0.18 deg RMS · VR Cinematics kit
pool.notes: Same comparison in motion, twenty seconds, looped. Watch the horizon on the left. This take is a seeded practice take built to have the same problems as a real recording, so every student has the identical numbers.

Measured, not eyeballed. On the class practice take: jitter is the RMS of what a 0.05 second Gaussian would remove, 1.54 degrees before and 0.18 after. Angular acceleration is the seasick number: 2575 degrees per second squared before, 136 after. Residual roll goes from 13.3 degrees to zero. Everyone will run the measure tool on their own copy and should see the same dialog. These numbers are from the seeded 20 second take at 90 Hz, verified on UE 5.8.2.

pool.title:
Capture
It.
pool.tagline: Take Recorder keeps what you add. Replay keeps the world.
pool.notes: Part two, run of show 0:20 to 0:45. Three ways to get a take, and which one you want.

pool.title: Three Ways to Get a Take
pool.subtitle: Pick by what you need to re-shoot

items.t:
Pawn as a source;
head = Camera component

Whole game state:
physics, NPCs, FX

Admin install once:
do it the day before

pool.notes: Three routes. Take Recorder keeps transforms and animation for the sources you add: add the VR pawn while you're in VR Preview or PIE, and set the take frame rate to the headset rate, 90. The recorded head is a Camera component with a relative transform under the pawn root, so the class tool reads it in world space by scrubbing Sequencer. The Replay system keeps game state, so physics, NPCs and effects play back and you can fly any camera through it, but only replicated actors are recorded, and replay of VR head and hands is documented in the kit as untested. Meta XR Simulator drives the same OpenXR session from keyboard and mouse and has a Record and Replay capture, but its activation script writes a machine-wide OpenXR registry key and needs elevation, so install it the day before. ALEX TO CONFIRM: Meta XR plugin on stock 5.8 has an open Meta bug that modules fail to load; the kit lists it as untested.

Say this out loud early. The practice take is built to have the same four problems as a real recording, and Build practice stage and take regenerates the identical seeded take for anyone whose numbers differ. Anything we do today works on it. Run of show 0:32.

pool.title:
Stabilize
It.
pool.notes: Part three, run of show 0:50 to 1:10. Do it by hand once so the one-click version is not magic.

Idea one. Don't filter three Euler curves. They break near yaw 180 and at steep pitch, which is exactly where players look. Convert to quaternions, flip signs so neighbors agree, because q and minus q are the same rotation and averaging across a sign flip collapses to zero. Filter the four components, renormalize, convert back, and unwrap yaw so keys never jump from 359 to 0, which Sequencer would render as a full spin. Use a zero-phase filter: offline there is no reason to accept lag, and a lagging POV turns after the player did.

pool.title:
Never Smooth
Across a Teleport
pool.subtitle: Idea two: segment first, then filter
pool.alt: A diagram: the true camera path jumps at a teleport; a filter run across the jump starts drifting about ten frames early, while a filter run on each segment does not.
bullets: Teleports and snap turns move faster than any head can: over 8 m/s or 1000 °/s
A 45° snap turn at 90 Hz is about 4000 °/s
Smooth each segment on its own, then cut on the jump: a cut hides it for free
Measured on the class take: over 30 cm off the true path 10 frames early, versus under 3 cm segmented
pool.notes: Idea two, and the one most students have never seen. If you run a filter across a teleport, the camera starts drifting toward the destination about ten frames before the jump: a swoop through the set. On the class take it was more than 30 centimeters off the true path ten frames early, against under 3 centimeters when each segment is filtered separately. The class tool finds discontinuities with thresholds of 8 meters per second and 1000 degrees per second. Then it marks them with TAKE CUT markers, and you cut on those frames. Never cut anywhere else.

pool.bigText:
Level the horizon.
Nobody misses the roll.
pool.notes: Idea three. Scale the residual roll toward zero. Roll is the biggest nausea source in head-camera footage and viewers do not miss it. On the class take it goes from 13.3 degrees to zero. One caution: a head-centered path from an avatar head bone needs about 14 centimeters of forward offset, or the POV renders from inside the head mesh. Take Recorder's HMD camera is already at the eyes.

pool.bigText:
By hand:
Curve Editor → Filter Tool
pool.notes: Students follow along here. Open the take's Camera or VR_Head transform curves in the Curve Editor, select the rotation channels, run the Euler filter first, then a Gaussian or an FFT low-pass. It works, per channel, and it is blind to teleports, which is why we then do the one-click version. Epic ships its own scripted version at Engine/Plugins/VirtualProduction/VirtualCamera/Content/Python/VCamSmooth.py: Bake plus Gaussian. Run of show 0:50.

pool.notes: The five rigs the Re-shoot command builds on your take: stabilized POV at 12 millimeters, about 90 degrees horizontal; over-shoulder at 24; orbit at 35; locked-off tripod at 50; low hero at 18. Click through them. Each one is an ordinary CineCamera: right-click it and Pilot it to show it is just keys. The command also builds a first-pass edit in the Camera Cuts track, cutting on the TAKE CUT markers. The rig descriptions beyond the lens are my film-grammar shorthand, not measured claims. Run of show 1:10.

Make it yours, run of show 1:20: re-time the Camera Cuts track, swap a shot to another camera, add one hand-keyed camera move. The rule is simple: always cut at a TAKE CUT marker. Those are the frames where the player teleported or snap turned, and a cut hides that jump for free. Every student should leave with a cut that differs from yours.

pool.title: Find the Shot Before You Fly
pool.subtitle: Drag the camera. Pick a lens. Take the shot.
pool.badge: Concept demo, built for the MIA talk
pool.notes: A concept demo, built for the Rome talk, so you can try the idea without a headset. A simple set: two actors, a lamp, a backdrop. Drag the camera on the plan, switch to an 85 millimeter lens and the framing tightens, put on a 2.39 mask, take a wide, a two-shot and a close-up. That's a shot list made before anyone flies anywhere. It needs WebGL; if the machine lacks it, the slide says so and you skip it. Say concept demo, never product.

pool.title:
Render
It.
pool.notes: Part five, run of show 1:35 to 1:55. Start a draft render early so it is running while you talk.

pool.title: Draft Fast, Final Once
pool.subtitle: Same sequence, two presets

items.t:
Real motion blur
from 90 Hz keys

pool.notes: The kit has a Draft preset and a Final preset. Draft is 720p and finished a 600 frame edit in about 75 seconds including startup on the Toaster test machine, a GTX 1080 Ti on UE 5.8.2; Final is 1080p with 8 temporal samples and took about 4 minutes. Don't render the final live: play the pre-rendered file. The first render compiles shaders, about a minute, so do it in pre-flight. The Show command-line render menu item prints the command to render in a second process or on another machine. Movie Render Graph is the same settings as nodes: first segment to cut if you run late. Don't demo the path tracer: it needs hardware ray tracing and many student machines can't run it.

pool.title: The Three Render Traps
pool.subtitle: Every one exits cleanly and writes nothing useful
pool.alt: A contact sheet: three frames from each of the five camera rigs, each labeled with its rig and frame number.
bullets: Zero frames: the output frame rate is below the sequence rate
Empty file names: {sequence_name} expands to nothing on the legacy command-line path
Black frames: an untitled level, or no Camera Cuts track
pool.notes: Three traps that all look like success. Zero frames: the output frame rate is below the sequence's. Empty file names: on the legacy command-line preset path in 5.8.2, the sequence name token resolves to an empty string and frames land in Saved/MovieRenders named .0000.png, so write the sequence name literally into the preset. Black frames: an untitled level cannot render, or the sequence has no Camera Cuts track, or every cut points at a missing camera. The contact sheet is the check: look at the start, middle and end frame of every shot before you trust a render.

pool.bigText:
Open the shutter
at the frame.
pool.notes: A subtle one, for people rendering with temporal samples. The default shutter centers on the frame time, so on the first frame after a teleport or snap turn half the sub-samples see the old pose and half the new, and MRQ averages them into a see-through double exposure. Set MoviePipelineCameraSetting shutter_timing to FRAME_OPEN: the shutter opens at the frame and integrates forward, so a cut on the jump never ghosts. Verified on 5.8.2: frames on both sides of the snap turn and the teleport were clean single exposures, and real motion blur survived on a pan. In Movie Render Graph it is the camera node's ShutterTiming. Draft renders with one temporal sample can't show this, so check the final preset's shot-start frames.

pool.notes: Four generations of camera tooling on one show. 2023: MagicCam, a Blueprint that calls shot presets from the keyboard. December 2025, the final run: a livestream with a human cinematographer directing, and cameras generated procedurally for specific characters. Then the show recorded as data, so the camera is free after the fact. And in October 2026 a cinematographer build that lets visitors shoot new coverage of the recording and assemble a working cut. Each generation made the previous one's assumption obvious: a camera is a rig you place, then a shot you call, then a decision you can revisit. The 2023 stop is dated from the Blueprint's last-saved version (December 2023); earlier seasons had cameras too, and I did not document them. ALEX TO CONFIRM.

pool.title: MagicCam: A Shot Is a Struct
pool.subtitle: A Christmas Carol VR, 2023, Unreal Engine 5.2
pool.alt: A card showing a shot preset as a struct with height, distance, rotation, performers and MetaHuman sockets, and the keys that call presets.
bullets: Keys 0–9 and Alt+0–9 call SetCam0 to SetCam13; PageUp and PageDown cycle
Each preset is one struct: height, distance, rotation, who to look at, which sockets
Two-shot compositions: “Character A on Left, Character B on Right”
Height comes off a MetaHuman face socket, so the framing follows the performer
pool.notes: The 2023 camera Blueprint is called BP_MagicCamera. 601 nodes. Keys 0 to 9 and Alt combinations call SetCam0 through SetCam13, and PageUp and PageDown cycle through them. Every preset calls one macro, CamSet, with a struct: a height offset, a distance, a rotation, which performer to look at, which performer to snap to, left and right axis sockets, a socket to look at, a socket to offset from, and a look-at offset. The sockets are MetaHuman face sockets such as FACIAL_C_NoseTip, which is how a camera framed for a short performer stays framed for a tall one. The comment on the macro says Character A on the left, Character B on the right: these are two-shot compositions. The lesson for your project: make the shot a data structure, and have the key press just select one. The struct field list is exact; the card's wording of each field is a paraphrase of the Blueprint's pin names. Read from Alex's pasted T3D export with the blueprint-reader, not from the live project.

pool.title: Damped Follow, and a Camera That Never Frames Nothing
pool.subtitle: The rest of MagicCam
pool.alt: The ghost of Jacob Marley in A Christmas Carol VR
bullets: Toggles for distance damping and look-at; a damping of zero is a hard cut
On a camera switch it waits 0.2 s, then snaps the damping to its target
Distance and height scale with the performer’s Z scale × 0.8
A hidden performer is swapped for an invisible “dummy Marley head”, so a camera never frames an empty spot
pool.notes: Three details from the same Blueprint that are worth stealing. A damped follow with toggles for distance damping and look-at, where a damping value of zero is a hard cut. On a camera switch it waits 0.2 seconds and then sets the actual damping equal to the target, so the new shot doesn't glide in from the old one. Distance and height are scaled by the performer's Z scale times 0.8. And a hidden performer is swapped for an invisible dummy Marley head, so a preset that frames a character who is currently offstage still has something to frame. The 2026 notes list the same guard as a port worth making: jump and preset targets should skip hidden characters.

pool.notes: For the final December 2025 run we livestreamed it. A human cinematographer, Jackie, directed the stream. Alex captured supplementary footage and documentation on a separate path while she did. The tools, per Alex's December 21, 2025 walkthrough video: cameras generated procedurally for specific characters, the virtual camera system, OBS for recording, and a custom console command that toggles audience member names, so the stream can show a name or not. He also notes the platform can capture and replay audience interactions, which isn't common in other platforms. ALEX TO CONFIRM: this slide is built from the one-line summary of that video in the knowledge base, not from the project; confirm which cameras were procedural and what 'supplementary footage' means before teaching it as a recipe.

pool.title: Replay: Any Seat in the House
pool.alt: A recorded performance played back in the replay system: Marley’s ghost confronts Scrooge, seen from a free camera with the replay controls on screen.
pool.credit: Replay recording of a performance · A Christmas Carol VR · Yu-Jun Yeh
pool.notes: Here is the replay system. We recorded the performances as data, using Unreal's replay recording of the live session: the motion capture, the cues and the spatial audio, not video. That means the camera is free after the fact. Scrub the timeline, fly anywhere, and see the controls on screen. Everything after this slide is about what it took to make a free camera in a replay actually reliable.

pool.title: Replay Playback Will Bite You
pool.subtitle: Four fixes from the 2026 camera build (UE 5.4)
pool.alt: A scene from A Christmas Carol VR
bullets: RepNotifies fire before BeginPlay on the first bunch: re-apply values at the end of BeginPlay
A replay viewer is a client, so live-session watchdogs run and eject you: gate them on “is playing replay”
Seek cooldown: time it from the completion callback, not the start
Pause by setting a world pauser: demo time and audio stop, the camera keeps flying
pool.notes: Four things any project that plays back DemoNetDriver replays will hit; we found them in the 2024 project on UE 5.4. One: on the first bunch, RepNotifies run before BeginPlay, so anything BeginPlay creates, like a dynamic material or a widget, isn't there yet. The symptom was every avatar the same green with no name until you skipped once. Fix: re-apply the replicated values at the end of BeginPlay. Two: a replay viewer is a client, so a live-session watchdog that watches a server heartbeat stalls during a seek or a long pause, and then calls JoinSession and kicks you out of the replay. 'Pressing skip too fast crashes it' was really one seek. Fix: gate every reconnect on is-playing-replay. Three: don't start another seek until about 30 frames and three-quarters of a second after the previous seek's completion callback. Four: there is no demopause command in 5.4; setting any PlayerState as the world pauser stops demo time and sound while the spectator camera keeps flying. These are from our KB technique note and verified in PIE on the 2024 project; your engine version and project may differ.

pool.bigText:
A seek can bring back
a scene that's gone.
pool.notes: A beautiful one. When we sought into a beat where Dickens's parlor had already vanished, the replay restored the streamed-out parlor for about four seconds and replayed its dissolve, in the middle of someone's shot. Our fix is unglamorous: a five second pre-roll under a black card. The cut starts, you see black, the world settles, then the shot begins. Replay won't reconstruct streamed scenes on a seek, so design the edit around it.

pool.title: The Cinematographer Build
pool.subtitle: ACCVRCinematographer plugin, UE 5.4.4, October 2026
pool.alt: Key art for A Christmas Carol VR
bullets: Pause keeps the camera live; a seek guard; an Xbox map where every button does something documented
Shot slots with 24, 35, 50 and 85 mm lens presets, saved to JSON
A whole-show working cut: scenes named from the show’s act and cue, credits, crash-safe saves, export
Weak edit, cut and loop, to review a cut in place
pool.notes: Last week's build, for a demo table at the MIA market in Rome. A plugin on top of the replay: pause that keeps the camera flying, the seek guard from the previous slide, and a gamepad map. Shot slots with lens presets of 24, 35, 50 and 85 millimeters, saved to a JSON file so a crash doesn't lose your shots. Then the redesign Alex asked for after testing the first version: a whole-show working cut, with scenes that start and end, named automatically from the show's act and cue, a Shot by credit on each shot, a title card, crash-safe saves and an export. The first version was a three-shot beat around Scrooge's arrival; it was superseded in two days. ALEX TO CONFIRM: it is built and playtested in PIE and packaged as SVN revision 849, but a physical gamepad hold and whether the audio sounds continuous through a cut had not been checked by a person when this was written, and the laptop that holds anything newer than r849 was offline. Say prototype, never product.

pool.title: The Title Card Is a Decision
pool.subtitle: What to call it, and who gets the credit
pool.alt: A black 2.39 title card: A CHRISTMAS CAROL VR, WORKING CUT with version and date, the scene, Shot by names, and Performed live by Ari Tarr and Debbie Deer, Work in progress.
bullets: “Director’s Cut” means the director’s own version: the wrong label
“Working cut” plus a version number is the honest one
Credit “Shot by”, not “DP”: visitors frame and cut, they don’t light
The version goes up per export, not per edit
pool.notes: A small decision that took research and is worth showing, because it's the same thinking as naming a render. Editing stages run assembly, rough cut, fine cut, picture lock; an unfinished film shown to an audience is a work-in-progress screening; a delivery head slate carries the title, version, date and running time. Director's Cut would have claimed the director made it. For the credit: a DP sets the look and runs camera and lighting crews, a camera operator frames, an editor decides when to cut. Visitors frame, choose the lens, and choose the cuts, but light nothing, and many people don't know the abbreviation DP. So the on-screen credit is Shot by, followed by names. The card shown is the template; the fields in angle brackets are filled per cut. Decision record: 2026-10-22.

We wanted a phone-as-camera feel in the cut. Findings: UE 5.1 moved the VirtualCamera plugin to Runtime, but the 5.4 docs still call it the in-editor Virtual Camera system; Live Link in a packaged game needs the messaging flag and Shipping is unsupported; and an Epic staff reply on a 2024 forum thread confirmed that enabling a VCam actor crashes a packaged build because it loads editor-only code. So in the project, V toggles the level's VCam component, the cinematographer plugin reads it by reflection with no module dependency, and packaged builds are unaffected and use the normal camera. That is the 5.4.4 answer. ALEX TO CONFIRM: not re-tested on 5.8, which is what this class uses; check before telling students it works or doesn't.

pool.bigText:
Cameras are data.
Shots are structs.
Credit the operator.
pool.notes: The three things to take from five winters of cameras. Cameras are data: whether it's a Blueprint struct, a JSON file of shot slots, or a recorded replay, if the shot is data you can change your mind afterwards. Shots are structs: the key press only selects. And credit the operator: the moment a visitor can make a shot, the title card and the credit become part of the design.
